questions.question: Discuss delayed coking and its advantages.
questions.solution_html:
• Delayed coking is a semi-batch thermal cracking process where preheated heavy oils are
  • sent to a coke drum, where cracking and coke formation take place. In this process, heavy
  • residual oil is cracked in coke drums to form solid coke and vapors. Solid coke remains in
  • the coke drum, once full, the drum is cooled and the solid coke is cut out. Stream and
  • volatiles escape from the coke drum is again fed to the fractionator. These vapors give heat
  • to the incoming fed and it contain valuable light hydrocarbons. Delayed coking controls
  • the coke formation inside large coke drums, ensures better heat management, gives higher
  • yield of liquid products, and allows continuous operation with periodic coke removal.
  • ((2 marks) each for explanation and any (2 marks) for advantages)
  • smaller ones using a suitable catalyst, typically a zeolite-based material. The process occurs at
  • relatively lower temperatures and pressures compared to thermal cracking, due to the presence
  • of the catalyst which promotes efficient bond breaking and rearrangement of hydrocarbon
  • chains. Catalytic cracking proceeds via ionic mechanism involving formation of carbocation.
  • There are 3 types of catalytic cracking processes- fixed bed cracking, moving bed process
  • fluidised bed process. The most common industrial unit used today is the Fluidized Catalytic
  • Cracking, which allows continuous catalyst regeneration and high conversion rates. Advantages
  • Catalytically cracked gasoline consists of isoparaffins and aromatics which are chemically
  • stable than gasoline obtained from thermal cracking. Catalytically cracked gasoline has high
  • octane number. Sulphur content of catalytically cracked gasoline is lower than thermally
  • cracked gasoline. Catalytic cracking gives rise to lesser number of residues.
  • (Catalytic cracking, its advantages and applications give (5 marks) each)
  • Hydrocracking (minor reaction)

questions.question: Discuss the limitations of fixed bed and moving bed processes and how / fluidized bed cracking overcomes them.
questions.solution_html:
• cracking overcomes them.
  • Fixed bed catalyst: Continuous operation is not possible (requires shutdown for regeneration).
  • Limited catalyst utilization. Not suitable for continuous large-scale operations.
  • Moving bed catalyst: Complex design and higher cost. Catalyst attrition (wear and tear) due
  • to movement. Possibility of catalyst loss or contamination during movement
  • Fluidized Bed Cracking Overcomes these Limitations
  • Provides continuous catalyst regeneration, maintaining high activity. Ensures better mixing
  • and contact between feed and catalyst, improving cracking efficiency. Allows uniform
  • temperature control and smoother operation, leading to higher yield and process stability.
  • Catalyst regeneration without shutdown. ((2 marks) each for the limitations of fixed bed and
  • moving bed and (3 marks) for advantages of fluidized bed cracking- ANY 2 points for each process)
questions.final_answer: moving bed and for advantages of fluidized bed cracking- ANY 2 points for each process)

questions.question: Discuss the desirable properties of commercial hydrocracking catalysts.
questions.solution_html:
• Catalyst type and activity are crucial, as hydrocracking uses bifunctional catalysts with both
  • acidic and hydrogenation functions, and their activity determines selectivity and yield. The
  • catalyst should efficiently promote both cracking and hydrogenation reactions under moderate
  • temperature and pressure. It should selectively produce desired products such as middle
  • distillates (diesel, kerosene) with minimal unwanted by-products. The catalyst must withstand
  • high temperatures, pressures, and mechanical stress without breaking down. It should resist
  • deactivation by impurities such as sulfur, nitrogen, and metals present in the feedstock. (Any
  • FIVE Points Give (7 Marks))

questions.question: Explain the manufacture of petroleum coke by thermal cracking.
questions.solution_html:
• Thermal cracking is a non-catalytic process in which heavy petroleum fractions (like vacuum
  • residue) are broken into lighter hydrocarbons and solid coke by applying high temperature and
  • pressure in the absence of oxygen. This process is done in Dubs cracking unit. These units
  • have 2 sections and it is consisting of evaporators and coke drums. The feed is initially
  • preheated in a furnace to a temperature of around 450–500°C. The heated feed then enters a
  • coke drum or reaction chamber, where thermal cracking takes place. Due to the high
  • temperature, the large hydrocarbon molecules break down into lighter fractions such as gases
  • oils, and solid coke. Importantly, the process is carried out in the absence of air to prevent
  • combustion. The vapor products from the cracking reaction are directed to a fractionating
  • tower, where they are separated into different components such as LPG, gasoline, diesel, and
  • gas oil, while the solid coke settles at the bottom of the drum. Once the coke drum becomes
  • full, it is cooled, and the accumulated coke is removed using high-pressure water jets. The

  • rhodium) are used instead of cobalt catalysts. The reaction involves the addition of carbon
  • monoxide and hydrogen to an olefin to produce aldehydes. The process operates at lower

  • times faster than the conventional process. The ratio of normal to iso aldehyde is16:1 more
  • over catalyst can be recovered completely. The rhodium-catalyzed modified hydroformylation
  • process offers higher yield, better selectivity, and lower operating costs compared to the older
  • cobalt-catalyzed process. (Explanation of modified method (5 marks) & Proper explanation of the
  • 2nd part (2 marks))

  • Produces fatty alcohols, which are key raw materials for detergents, surfactants, and

questions.question: Explain the role of syngas and aromatic compounds in the / petrochemical industry.
questions.solution_html:
• Syngas provides basic building blocks for many chemical syntheses.
  • Syngas is a mixture of carbon monoxide (CO) and hydrogen (H₂) and is produced by gasifying
  • carbon-based feedstocks (e.g., coal, natural gas, biomass).
  • Products Derived from Syngas
  • Methanol (CH₃OH): Used in producing chemicals like formaldehyde, acetic acid, and plastics.
  • Ammonia (NH₃): used to produce fertilizers, explosives, and plastics.
  • Aromatics: Aromatic hydrocarbons such as benzene, toluene, and xylenes are produced
  • primarily through the refining of naphtha or by catalytic reforming of petroleum.
  • Products Derived from Aromatics
  • Benzene (C₆H₆): Used in the production of styrene (for polystyrene), phenol, cyclohexane, and
  • nylon. Toluene (C₆H₅CH₃): Solvent, and a precursor to benzene, xylene, and toluene
  • diisocyanate (used in polyurethane production). Xylene (C₆H₄(CH₃)₂): Used in the production
  • of polyester fibers, solvents, and paints. (3 points each from syn gas and aromatics (7 marks))
questions.final_answer: of polyester fibers, solvents, and paints. (3 points each from syn gas and aromatics )
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025
